questions.question: State Dalton's atomic theory. Write two of its drawbacks.
questions.solution:
**Dalton (1808):** (1) matter consists of indivisible atoms; (2) atoms of an element are identical; (3) compounds form by simple whole-number union of atoms; (4) atoms are indestructible in reactions.

**Drawbacks:** atoms ARE divisible (electrons, protons, neutrons); atoms of an element differ (isotopes); the theory cannot explain bonding or spectra.
questions.knowledgeNote: Dalton explained the laws of chemical combination — the next questions' topic — but isotopes and subatomic particles broke his indivisibility.
questions.answer: **Dalton's atomic theory:** (1) matter consists of tiny indivisible particles called **atoms**; (2) atoms of a given element are **identical** in mass and properties; (3) atoms of different elements differ in mass and properties; (4) compounds form when atoms **combine in small whole-number ratios**; (5) atoms are **neither created nor destroyed** in chemical reactions — only rearranged. **Two drawbacks:** (1) atoms **are divisible** — they contain subatomic particles (electrons, protons, neutrons); (2) atoms of the same element are **not all identical** — isotopes differ in mass. (Also: his theory could not explain why atoms bond, and treated matter as purely particulate, ignoring the wave nature later revealed.) **Deep point:** the theory's five postulates are right about combination ratios and conservation — its failures are precisely the two discoveries of the next century, the electron and the isotope.

questions.question: State the law of multiple proportions and illustrate it with carbon oxides.
questions.solution:
When two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element combining with a fixed mass of the other are in a small whole-number ratio.

CO: 12 g C joins 16 g O. CO₂: 12 g C joins 32 g O. Oxygen masses 16:32 = **1:2**.
questions.knowledgeNote: Definite proportions (one compound, fixed ratio) vs multiple proportions (several compounds, ratio of ratios) — NEB asks the pair together.
questions.answer: **Law of multiple proportions:** when two elements combine to form **more than one compound**, the masses of one element that combine with a **fixed mass** of the other are in a ratio of **small whole numbers**. **Carbon oxides:** in CO, 16 g of oxygen combines with 12 g of carbon; in CO₂, 32 g of oxygen combines with 12 g of carbon. **With carbon fixed at 12 g, the oxygen masses are 16 : 32 = 1 : 2** — a small whole-number ratio, exactly as the law requires (the extra oxygen in CO₂ is exactly double). **Deep point:** the law is the chemical evidence for atoms — whole-number ratios are what discrete, identical particles must produce.

questions.question: State Avogadro's law and write two of its applications.
questions.solution:
**Avogadro's law:** equal volumes of gases at the same T and P contain equal numbers of molecules.

**Applications:** (1) proves diatomic nature of H₂, O₂, N₂ (Gay-Lussac volumes need it); (2) fixes atomic weights via vapour density (M = 2 × VD); (3) 1 mole of any gas occupies 22.4 L at STP.
questions.knowledgeNote: Avogadro reconciled Gay-Lussac's volume ratios with Dalton — H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl needs diatomic molecules.
questions.answer: **Avogadro's law:** equal volumes of all gases, at the same temperature and pressure, contain **equal numbers of molecules** (V ∝ n at fixed T, P). **Two applications:** (1) **molar volume** — one mole of any ideal gas occupies 22.4 L at STP, the bridge between gas volume and moles in every stoichiometric calculation; (2) **deducing molecular formulae** — combining Gay-Lussac's law of gaseous volumes with Avogadro's law proved that hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen etc. are **diatomic molecules** (e.g. 1 volume H₂ + 1 volume Cl₂ → 2 volumes HCl forces H₂ and Cl₂ to contain 2 atoms each), settling the atomic-mass scale. **Deep point:** the law is why chemistry can count by measuring volume — for gases, the measuring cylinder is a particle counter.

questions.question: Calculate the number of atoms in 5.6 g of iron. (Fe = 56)
questions.knowledgeNote: Grams → moles (÷ atomic mass) → particles (× Avogadro) is the universal two-step chain.
questions.answer: **Moles of Fe:** n = m/M = 5.6 g / 56 g/mol = 0.1 mol. **Atoms:** N = n × N_A = 0.1 × 6.022 × 10²³ = **6.022 × 10²² atoms**. **Deep point:** the two-step bridge — grams → moles → particles — is the single most-used chain in chemistry; the mole ratio (0.1) is the number worth checking before touching the exponent.

questions.question: Calculate the percentage of nitrogen in urea, CO(NH₂)₂. (C = 12, O = 16, N = 14, H = 1)
questions.solution:
Molar mass = 12 + 16 + 2(14 + 2) = 60 g/mol. Nitrogen mass = 28 g.

%N = (28/60) × 100 ≈ **46.7%** — the highest N-content of common fertilisers, which is why urea dominates the market.
questions.knowledgeNote: % composition = (total mass of element / molar mass) × 100 — the same step that starts every empirical-formula problem.
questions.answer: **Molar mass of urea:** CO(NH₂)₂ = 12 + 16 + 2(14 + 2×1) = 12 + 16 + 32 = **60 g/mol**. **Mass of N per mole:** 2 × 14 = 28 g. **Percentage:** %N = (28/60) × 100 = **46.67% ≈ 46.7%**. **Deep point:** the 46% figure is why urea rules the fertiliser market — every stoichiometry here is an economics argument in disguise.

questions.question: State Gay-Lussac's law of gaseous volumes with one example.
questions.solution:
When gases react at the same T and P, their volumes are in a small whole-number ratio.

**Example:** 1 vol H₂ + 1 vol Cl₂ → 2 vol HCl (1:1:2).
questions.knowledgeNote: Volume ratios mirror molecule ratios — the law only works for gases, never for solids or liquids.
questions.answer: **Gay-Lussac's law of gaseous volumes:** when gases react (or are produced) at the same temperature and pressure, the **volumes of the gaseous reactants and products are in simple whole-number ratios**. **Example:** 1 volume of hydrogen + 1 volume of chlorine → 2 volumes of hydrogen chloride (H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl) — the ratio 1 : 1 : 2; similarly 2 volumes H₂ + 1 volume O₂ → 2 volumes steam (2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O). **Deep point:** the law is Avogadro's law's experimental half — simple volume ratios are only possible because equal volumes hold equal numbers of molecules.
